newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian rupiah slumps, pulls down others.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian rupiah slumps, pulls down others.

text.p: The Indonesian rupiah slumped and pulled down other Southeast Asian currencies on Thursday after Bank Indonesia (BI) scrapped the daily announcement of its intervention band.

The timing of the action by the Indonesian central bank, seen as amounting to a managed float of the currency, came as a surprise a day after it raised rates and sold dollars to keep the rupiah within its intervention band.
BI governor Sudradjad Djiwandono told a capital market conference the central bank's band move was only an adjustment to neighbouring countries.
The rupiah fell to a historic low of 2,765 after the announcement against its opening around 2,648/58. By 0430 GMT, it had stabilised around 2,750/80.

A state bank dealer in Jakarta said the statement did not imply the removal of the band, only its announcement. "This implies that the band will be invisible, allowing the central bank to intervene any time it wants," he said.
"Basically Bank Indonesia can intervene at any time. It's a good move," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian currency research at BZW Asia in Singapore.
"It's much more prudent than widening the band and giving the market a fresh target to aim at," he said.
"Doggedly defending the band would whittle away at the country's reserves, raise interest rates and slow growth."
He said it was not surprising that the rupiah had plunged on the announcement, but that there was scope for recovery later.
"We are going to see substantial over-shooting," Supple said. "But (the announcement) lays the conditions for reversal of the rupiah in the long-term and bring it back to a semblance of fair value."
Other Southeast Asian currencies, which started the day on relatively firm footing following the dollar's overnight drop against the majors, fell along with the rupiah.
"The rupiah's the mover and shaker today. If dollar/rupiah does settle down, the rest of the (dollar/)Asians should top out too," a U.S. bank dealer said.

Comments by Malaysian Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim exacerbated pressure on the ringgit. He said the government was concerned about the sharp rise in Malaysia's June trade deficit to 2.8 billion ringgit and it may use taxes or fiscal measures to cut imports and stimulate exports.

But his remark that the government need not cancel major infrastructure projects caused confusion a day after Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said plans for large projects would be reviewed following the ringgit's steep decline.
The ringgit fell from a high of 2.7530 to the dollar after the remarks. It was quoted at 2.7720/70 at 0430 GMT but dealers said it remained vulnerable to more weakness.
The Singapore dollar slipped back through the 1.51 level against the U.S. dollar and the Thai baht also came under pressure, partly from commercial dollar demand, but dealers said activity was muted.
The baht was at 31.50/31.60 to the dollar onshore against 31.43/31.55 late on Wednesday. It was at 31.25/35 offshore.
The Philippine peso recovered from an early low of 29.620 to the dollar, but remained fragile after the central bank cut its rates amid persistent demand for dollars.
The overnight borrowing rate was cut by four percentage points to 14 percent and liquidity reserves raised to five percent from four percent to moderate the impact on the peso.
The Taiwan dollar was largely steady on suspected intervention by the central bank to sell U.S. dollars at T$28.727. It was seen trading in a narrow T$28.70-75 range.
